chapters.title: Physics and Measurement
chapters.description: What physics studies and how we measure physical quantities using SI units.

lessons.title: Physical Quantities and Measurement
lessons.summary: Learn what physics is, the difference between fundamental and derived quantities, and how to measure and convert SI units correctly.

sections.title: Why physics begins with measurement
sections.body:
**Physics** is the science that studies matter, energy, and how they interact. From a falling mango to the electricity in your home, physics explains *why* things happen.

To describe nature, scientists must **measure**. **Measurement** is comparing an unknown quantity with an agreed standard. If a farmer near Bahir Dar says a field is "20 paces" long, that means something different for a tall person and a short person. So scientists everywhere agreed to use one shared system, the **SI system** (International System of Units), so a measurement in Addis Ababa means exactly the same in any country.

sections.title: What you will learn
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- Explain what **physics** studies.
- Name the seven **fundamental (base) quantities** and their SI units.
- Build **derived quantities** from base quantities.
- Use **prefixes** (kilo, centi, milli) to convert units.
- Tell the difference between **accuracy** and **precision**.
- Use **scientific notation** for very large or very small numbers.

sections.title: Fundamental and derived quantities
sections.body:
A **physical quantity** is anything we can measure. Quantities split into two groups.

**1. Fundamental (base) quantities** cannot be built from any other quantity. There are seven:

| Quantity | SI Unit | Symbol |
|---|---|---|
| Length | metre | m |
| Mass | kilogram | kg |
| Time | second | s |
| Temperature | kelvin | K |
| Electric current | ampere | A |
| Amount of substance | mole | mol |
| Luminous intensity | candela | cd |

**2. Derived quantities** are made by combining base quantities. For example:

- **Area** = length × width → m²
- **Volume** = length × width × height → m³
- **Speed** = distance ÷ time → m/s
- **Density** = mass ÷ volume → kg/m³

**Why does a shared system matter?** Because science is built on results that other people can check. If everyone uses the same units, an experiment can be repeated and trusted anywhere.

**Prefixes** are short ways to write very large or small numbers:

| Prefix | Symbol | Means |
|---|---|---|
| kilo | k | 1000 |
| centi | c | 0.01 |
| milli | m | 0.001 |

Useful conversions: 1 km = 1000 m, 1 m = 100 cm, 1 cm = 10 mm, 1 kg = 1000 g, 1 hour = 3600 s.

**Accuracy vs precision:** **Accuracy** is how close a measurement is to the true value. **Precision** is how close repeated measurements are to each other. You can be precise but not accurate (same wrong answer every time).

**Scientific notation** writes numbers as a value between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of ten, e.g. 300000 m/s = 3 × 10⁵ m/s.

sections.title: Worked example: unit conversion and density
sections.body:
**Question:** A block of metal has a mass of 2.4 kg and a volume of 300 cm³. Find its density in kg/m³.

**Step 1 — Write the formula.** Density = mass ÷ volume, so ρ = m / V.

**Step 2 — Convert volume to SI units.** 1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³, so:
300 cm³ ÷ 1 000 000 = 0.0003 m³ = 3 × 10⁻⁴ m³.

**Step 3 — Substitute the values with units.**
ρ = 2.4 kg ÷ 0.0003 m³

**Step 4 — Calculate.**
ρ = 8000 kg/m³

**Answer:** The density is **8000 kg/m³**. (This is close to iron, so the block could be iron.)

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body:
- **Forgetting the unit.** Writing "the length is 5" is wrong. Always write the number *and* the unit: 5 m.
- **Mixing cm and m in one calculation.** Convert everything to SI units first.
- **Wrong volume conversion.** 1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³, not 100 cm³. Cubing affects all three dimensions.
- **Confusing accuracy and precision.** Precise means *repeatable*; accurate means *correct*.
- **Multiplying when you should divide** when converting to a bigger unit.

sections.title: Memory tips
sections.body:
- **Smaller unit → bigger number, bigger unit → smaller number.**
- For cubic conversions, remember the **"power of three"**: 1 m = 100 cm, so 1 m³ = 100³ cm³ = 1 000 000 cm³.
- **Accuracy = Aim at the centre** (close to true value). **Precision = Points cluster** (readings close together).
- Dartboard picture: tight cluster off-centre = precise but not accurate.

sections.title: Practice questions
sections.body:
Try these, then check the answers.

**Q1.** Convert 4.5 km into metres.
**Q2.** Write 0.00056 m in scientific notation.
**Q3.** A stone has mass 0.6 kg and volume 2 × 10⁻⁴ m³. Find its density.

**Answers:**
1. 4.5 × 1000 = **4500 m**
2. **5.6 × 10⁻⁴ m**
3. ρ = 0.6 ÷ (2 × 10⁻⁴) = **3000 kg/m³**

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
- **Physics** studies matter, energy, and their interactions.
- **Measurement** compares an unknown quantity with a standard; always give a number **and** a unit.
- **Fundamental quantities** (7): length, mass, time, temperature, current, amount, luminous intensity.
- **Derived quantities** (area, volume, speed, density) come from base quantities.
- **Prefixes**: kilo = 1000, centi = 0.01, milli = 0.001.
- **Accuracy** = close to true value; **precision** = readings close to each other.
- **Density** ρ = m / V, measured in kg/m³.

questions.explanation: Time is a base quantity (SI unit second). Speed, area and density are derived from base quantities.

questions.prompt: What is the SI unit of mass?
questions.explanation: The kilogram (kg) is the SI base unit of mass. The gram is a smaller unit and the newton measures force.

A body has mass 600 g and volume 200 cm³. What is its density?
questions.explanation: Density = mass ÷ volume = 600 ÷ 200 = 3 g/cm³.

questions.explanation: The values are close to each other (precise) but far from 50 cm (not accurate).

questions.explanation: 1 m = 100 cm, so 1 m³ = 100 × 100 × 100 = 1 000 000 cm³. Cubing applies to all three dimensions.

chapters.title: Motion in a Straight Line
chapters.description: How to describe motion using distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration.

lessons.title: Describing Motion (Kinematics)
lessons.summary: Understand distance and displacement, speed and velocity, acceleration, and how to use the equations of uniformly accelerated motion.

sections.title: Everything is moving
sections.body:
A bus on the road to Hawassa, a runner on a track, the Earth around the Sun — everything moves. **Mechanics** is the part of physics that studies motion. The branch that *describes* motion without asking what causes it is called **kinematics**.

To describe motion clearly, we need careful words. Saying a car "went fast" is not enough. We need to know *how far*, *in which direction*, and *how the speed changed*. This lesson gives you the exact language and formulas physicists use.

sections.title: What you will learn
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- Distinguish **distance** from **displacement**.
- Distinguish **speed** from **velocity**.
- Define and calculate **acceleration**.
- Tell the difference between **scalar** and **vector** quantities.
- Use the **equations of uniformly accelerated motion**.
- Read a **velocity–time graph**.

sections.title: Distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration
sections.body:
Some quantities need only a size (number + unit); others also need a direction.

- A **scalar** has size only — e.g. distance, speed, time, mass.
- A **vector** has size *and* direction — e.g. displacement, velocity, acceleration, force.

**Distance** is the total path length travelled (a scalar). **Displacement** is the straight-line distance from start to finish, in a direction (a vector). If you walk 3 m east then 3 m west, the **distance** is 6 m but the **displacement** is 0 m, because you ended where you started.

**Speed** is how fast distance is covered: speed = distance ÷ time (scalar). **Velocity** is displacement ÷ time, with a direction (vector). The SI unit of both is **m/s**.

**Acceleration** is how quickly velocity changes:

**a = (v − u) / t**

where *u* = initial velocity, *v* = final velocity, *t* = time. The SI unit is **m/s²**. Speeding up gives positive acceleration; slowing down gives negative acceleration (also called **deceleration**).

**Why direction matters:** Forces and motion add up differently depending on direction. Treating velocity as a vector lets us correctly combine motions, which scalars alone cannot do.

**Equations of uniformly accelerated motion** (constant acceleration):

1. v = u + at
2. s = ut + ½at²
3. v² = u² + 2as

Here *s* is displacement. These three equations solve almost every straight-line motion problem at Grade 9.

sections.title: Velocity–time graph of a speeding-up car
sections.body: This graph shows a car whose velocity increases steadily from 0 to 8 m/s in 4 seconds. A straight, rising line means **constant acceleration**. The slope (rise ÷ run) gives the acceleration, and the area under the line gives the displacement.

sections.title: Worked example: a bus accelerating
sections.body:
**Question:** A bus starts from rest and reaches a velocity of 20 m/s in 10 s. Find (a) its acceleration and (b) the distance it travels in that time.

**Step 1 — List the data with units.**
u = 0 m/s (starts from rest), v = 20 m/s, t = 10 s.

**Step 2 — Find acceleration using a = (v − u)/t.**
a = (20 − 0) ÷ 10 = **2 m/s²**

**Step 3 — Find distance using s = ut + ½at².**
s = (0 × 10) + ½ × 2 × (10)²
s = 0 + ½ × 2 × 100
s = **100 m**

**Answer:** The acceleration is 2 m/s² and the bus travels 100 m.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body:
- **Confusing distance and displacement.** Distance is the whole path; displacement is start-to-finish straight line with direction.
- **Forgetting 'from rest' means u = 0.** Always read the question for the starting speed.
- **Squaring wrongly in s = ut + ½at².** The t² applies only to the second term.
- **Dropping the negative sign for deceleration.** Slowing down means a is negative.
- **Wrong units.** Acceleration is m/s², not m/s.

sections.title: Memory tips
sections.body:
- Remember the order of letters in **"v = u + at"**: **v**ery **u**seful **a**fter **t**ime.
- **Vector vs scalar:** a vector has a *direction* — picture an arrow. A scalar is just a number.
- On a **velocity–time graph**: **slope = acceleration**, **area = distance**.
- Deceleration = negative acceleration: "going down, sign goes down (−)."

sections.title: Practice questions
sections.body:
Try these, then check the answers.

**Q1.** A car speeds up from 5 m/s to 25 m/s in 4 s. Find its acceleration.
**Q2.** A cyclist travels 3 km north then 4 km north. What is the total displacement?
**Q3.** A stone is dropped from rest (a = 10 m/s²). How far does it fall in 3 s?

**Answers:**
1. a = (25 − 5) ÷ 4 = **5 m/s²**
2. 3 + 4 = **7 km north**
3. s = 0 + ½ × 10 × 3² = ½ × 10 × 9 = **45 m**

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
- **Kinematics** describes motion without asking its cause.
- **Scalar** = size only (distance, speed); **vector** = size + direction (displacement, velocity, acceleration).
- **Speed** = distance ÷ time; **velocity** = displacement ÷ time (m/s).
- **Acceleration** a = (v − u)/t, unit m/s².
- Equations of motion: v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as.
- On a velocity–time graph: slope = acceleration, area = displacement.

questions.explanation: Velocity has both size and direction, so it is a vector. Distance, speed and time are scalars.

questions.prompt: A car travels 150 m in 10 s. What is its average speed?
questions.explanation: Speed = distance ÷ time = 150 ÷ 10 = 15 m/s.

questions.prompt: A body speeds up from 4 m/s to 16 m/s in 6 s. What is its acceleration?
An object starts from rest and accelerates at 3 m/s² for 4 s. How far does it travel?
A person walks 5 m east, then 5 m west. What is the displacement?

chapters.title: Force and Newton's Laws of Motion
chapters.description: What forces are and how Newton's three laws explain motion and equilibrium.

lessons.title: Forces and Newton's Laws
lessons.summary: Learn about different types of forces, Newton's three laws of motion, and how to use F = ma and free-body diagrams.

sections.title: What makes things move or stop?
sections.body:
When you push a loaded cart at a market in Addis Ababa, it moves. When you stop pushing, it slows and stops. A **force** is a push or a pull. Forces can start motion, stop motion, change speed, change direction, or change the shape of an object.

Sir **Isaac Newton** discovered three simple laws that explain how forces affect motion. These **Newton's laws of motion** are some of the most important ideas in all of physics, and they still describe the motion of cars, footballs and rockets today.

sections.title: What you will learn
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- Define **force** and give its SI unit.
- Identify **contact** and **non-contact (field)** forces.
- State and explain **Newton's three laws of motion**.
- Use the formula **F = ma**.
- Explain the difference between **mass** and **weight**.
- Draw a simple **free-body diagram**.

sections.title: Force and the three laws
sections.body:
A **force** is a push or a pull, measured in **newtons (N)**. Forces are vectors, so direction matters.

Forces are of two kinds:
- **Contact forces** act by touching, e.g. friction, tension, the normal (support) force, applied push.
- **Non-contact (field) forces** act at a distance, e.g. gravity, magnetic force, electric force.

**Newton's First Law (Law of Inertia):** An object stays at rest, or keeps moving at constant velocity, unless an *unbalanced* force acts on it. **Inertia** is the tendency of an object to resist a change in its motion. This is why passengers lurch forward when a bus brakes suddenly.

**Newton's Second Law:** The acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force and inversely proportional to its mass:

**F = ma**

where F = net force (N), m = mass (kg), a = acceleration (m/s²). This law tells us *how much* an object accelerates.

**Newton's Third Law:** For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. When you push on the ground to walk, the ground pushes back on you with equal force.

**Mass vs weight:** **Mass** is the amount of matter in an object (kg) and never changes. **Weight** is the force of gravity on that mass: **W = mg**, where g ≈ 9.8 m/s² on Earth. Weight is measured in newtons and changes if gravity changes (you would weigh less on the Moon).

**Why F = ma works:** A bigger force gives a bigger acceleration; a heavier object is harder to accelerate. This single equation links force, mass and motion.

sections.title: Free-body diagram of a resting box
sections.body: A box sits still on a table. Its **weight** (gravity) pulls it down, and the **normal force** from the table pushes it up with equal strength. Because the two forces are balanced, the box stays at rest — exactly what Newton's First Law predicts.

sections.title: Worked example: force and weight
sections.body:
**Question:** A box of mass 5 kg is pushed with a net force of 20 N along a smooth floor. (a) Find its acceleration. (b) Find the weight of the box (take g = 9.8 m/s²).

**Step 1 — Find acceleration using F = ma.**
Rearrange: a = F ÷ m = 20 N ÷ 5 kg = **4 m/s²**

**Step 2 — Find weight using W = mg.**
W = 5 kg × 9.8 m/s² = **49 N**

**Answer:** The acceleration is 4 m/s² and the weight is 49 N.

**Note:** The mass stays 5 kg everywhere, but the weight would be different on the Moon because g is smaller there.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body:
- **Confusing mass and weight.** Mass is in kg and constant; weight is a force in newtons and depends on gravity.
- **Using total force instead of net force in F = ma.** Only the *unbalanced* force causes acceleration.
- **Thinking a moving object needs a constant force.** With no friction, no force is needed to keep constant velocity (First Law).
- **Forgetting forces are vectors.** Opposite forces subtract; same-direction forces add.
- **Mixing up action and reaction pairs** — they act on *different* objects.

sections.title: Memory tips
sections.body:
- **First law = lazy law:** objects are lazy and won't change motion on their own (inertia).
- **F = ma:** "Force Makes acceleration."
- **Weight = mass × g:** "We Make gravity" (W = mg).
- **Third law:** every push has a push-back — clap your hands and feel both.
- Mass is *matter* (kg); weight is a *force* (N) — both start differently for a reason.

sections.title: Practice questions
sections.body:
Try these, then check the answers (use g = 9.8 m/s²).

**Q1.** A 2 kg object accelerates at 5 m/s². What net force acts on it?
**Q2.** Find the weight of a 10 kg bag of teff on Earth.
**Q3.** A 1000 kg car is pushed by a net force of 3000 N. Find its acceleration.

**Answers:**
1. F = ma = 2 × 5 = **10 N**
2. W = mg = 10 × 9.8 = **98 N**
3. a = F/m = 3000 ÷ 1000 = **3 m/s²**

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
- A **force** is a push or pull, measured in **newtons (N)**; it is a vector.
- Forces are **contact** (friction, tension, normal) or **non-contact** (gravity, magnetism).
- **First Law:** without an unbalanced force, motion does not change (inertia).
- **Second Law:** F = ma (net force = mass × acceleration).
- **Third Law:** every action has an equal and opposite reaction.
- **Mass** (kg) is matter; **weight** W = mg (N) is the force of gravity.

A force that acts at a distance, e.g. gravity or magnetism.

The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms; constant everywhere.

questions.explanation: Force is measured in newtons (N). The kilogram is the unit of mass and the joule is the unit of energy.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a non-contact (field) force?
questions.explanation: Gravity acts at a distance without touching, so it is a non-contact force. Friction, tension and the normal force are contact forces.

questions.prompt: A net force of 12 N acts on a 3 kg object. What is its acceleration?
Using g = 10 m/s², what is the weight of a 6 kg object?
questions.explanation: Weight W = mg = 6 × 10 = 60 N.

questions.prompt: When a bus suddenly stops, passengers lurch forward. This is best explained by:
questions.explanation: By inertia (Newton's First Law), the passengers' bodies tend to keep moving forward even though the bus has stopped.

questions.prompt: An astronaut takes a 10 kg object to the Moon, where gravity is weaker. What happens to its mass and weight?
options: Mass stays the same, weight decreases
Mass decreases, weight stays the same
questions.explanation: Mass is the amount of matter and never changes (10 kg). Weight = mg, and since g is smaller on the Moon, the weight decreases.

chapters.title: Work, Energy and Power
chapters.description: How work, kinetic and potential energy, the conservation of energy, and power are related.

lessons.title: Work, Energy and Power
lessons.summary: Learn how to calculate work done, kinetic and potential energy, apply the conservation of energy, and find power.

sections.title: Energy makes things happen
sections.body:
When a farmer lifts a sack of grain, water rushes down the Blue Nile (Abay), or a lamp lights a room, **energy** is at work. **Energy** is the ability to do work, and it comes in many forms — movement, heat, light, electrical and chemical.

In everyday speech, "work" means any effort. In physics, **work** has an exact meaning: a force must move an object through a distance. This lesson shows how work, energy and power are connected by simple formulas.

sections.title: What you will learn
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- Define **work** and calculate it with W = F × d.
- Define **energy** and name its main forms.
- Calculate **kinetic energy** and **gravitational potential energy**.
- State the **law of conservation of energy**.
- Define and calculate **power**.
- Use the correct SI units: joule (J) and watt (W).

sections.title: Work, energy and power
sections.body:
**Work** is done when a force moves an object in the direction of the force:

**W = F × d**

where W = work (joules, J), F = force (N), d = distance moved in the direction of the force (m). If you push a wall and it does not move, you do **no work** in the physics sense, no matter how tired you feel.

**Energy** is the ability to do work, also measured in **joules (J)**. Two important mechanical forms are:

- **Kinetic energy (KE)** — energy of motion: **KE = ½mv²**, where m = mass (kg), v = speed (m/s).
- **Gravitational potential energy (PE)** — energy of height: **PE = mgh**, where h = height (m) and g ≈ 9.8 m/s².

**Law of conservation of energy:** Energy cannot be created or destroyed; it only changes from one form to another. The total energy stays the same. For example, when a stone falls, its potential energy changes into kinetic energy, but the total stays constant (ignoring air resistance).

**Power** is how fast work is done or energy is used:

**P = W / t**

where P = power (watts, W), W = work or energy (J), t = time (s). One watt means one joule per second. A more powerful machine does the same work in less time.

**Why these ideas matter:** Energy lets us compare very different processes — a moving car and a heated pot — using the same unit, the joule. Conservation of energy is one of the deepest rules in physics.

sections.title: Worked example: work, energy and power
sections.body:
**Question:** A worker lifts a 15 kg box to a shelf 2 m high in 3 s (take g = 10 m/s²). Find (a) the work done, (b) the potential energy gained, and (c) the power used.

**Step 1 — Find the lifting force.** To lift steadily, force = weight = mg = 15 × 10 = 150 N.

**Step 2 — Find the work done using W = F × d.**
W = 150 N × 2 m = **300 J**

**Step 3 — Find the potential energy gained using PE = mgh.**
PE = 15 × 10 × 2 = **300 J** (equal to the work done, as expected).

**Step 4 — Find the power using P = W / t.**
P = 300 J ÷ 3 s = **100 W**

**Answer:** Work = 300 J, PE gained = 300 J, power = 100 W.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body:
- **Thinking effort alone is work.** If the object does not move, no work is done in physics.
- **Forgetting the ½ in kinetic energy.** KE = ½mv², not mv².
- **Not squaring the speed.** The v in KE is squared, so doubling speed gives four times the KE.
- **Mixing up energy (J) and power (W).** Power is energy per second.
- **Using weight instead of mass (or vice versa)** in the formulas — check the units.

sections.title: Memory tips
sections.body:
- **Work = Force × distance:** "Work Forces Distance."
- **KE = ½mv²:** half of mass times velocity squared — remember the **½** and the **square**.
- **PE = mgh:** "My Greater Height" gives more potential energy.
- **Power = energy ÷ time:** more power = faster work. Watt = joule per second.
- No movement, no work — even if you sweat!

sections.title: Practice questions
sections.body:
Try these, then check the answers (use g = 10 m/s²).

**Q1.** A force of 50 N moves a crate 4 m. How much work is done?
**Q2.** A 2 kg ball moves at 3 m/s. Find its kinetic energy.
**Q3.** A motor does 600 J of work in 5 s. Find its power.

**Answers:**
1. W = F × d = 50 × 4 = **200 J**
2. KE = ½ × 2 × 3² = ½ × 2 × 9 = **9 J**
3. P = W/t = 600 ÷ 5 = **120 W**

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
- **Work** W = F × d, measured in **joules (J)**; no movement means no work.
- **Energy** is the ability to do work (J); forms include kinetic, potential, heat, light, electrical.
- **Kinetic energy** KE = ½mv²; **potential energy** PE = mgh.
- **Conservation of energy:** energy is never created or destroyed, only changed in form.
- **Power** P = W/t, measured in **watts (W)**; 1 W = 1 J/s.
- More power means the same work is done in less time.

chapters.title: Mechanical Properties of Fluids
chapters.description: Pressure in solids and liquids, atmospheric pressure, and how floating and density relate.

lessons.title: Pressure and Fluids
lessons.summary: Understand pressure in solids and liquids, atmospheric pressure, and why some objects float while others sink.

sections.title: Pushing on a surface
sections.body:
Why does a sharp knife cut more easily than a blunt one? Why do your feet sink into soft mud but not onto hard ground? The answer is **pressure**. A **fluid** is anything that can flow — both liquids and gases are fluids.

Pressure explains why dam walls, like those holding back water at the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, are built thicker at the bottom, and why we can drink through a straw. This lesson explains pressure in solids, liquids and the air around us.

sections.title: What you will learn
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- Define **pressure** and give its SI unit.
- Use the formula **P = F / A**.
- Explain how **pressure in a liquid** depends on depth and density.
- Describe **atmospheric pressure**.
- Explain **floating and sinking** using density and upthrust.

sections.title: Pressure in solids and liquids
sections.body:
**Pressure** is the force acting on each unit of area:

**P = F / A**

where P = pressure in **pascals (Pa)**, F = force (N), A = area (m²). One pascal is one newton per square metre.

For the same force, a **smaller area gives a larger pressure**. That is why a sharp knife (small area) cuts easily, and why wide tyres spread a vehicle's weight to stop it sinking into soft ground.

**Pressure in a liquid** increases with depth and density:

**P = ρgh**

where ρ = density of the liquid (kg/m³), g ≈ 9.8 m/s², h = depth (m). Liquid pressure acts in **all directions** and depends only on depth, not on the shape of the container. This is why a dam wall is thicker at the bottom, where the water pushes hardest.

**Atmospheric pressure** is the pressure caused by the weight of the air above us. At sea level it is about 101 000 Pa. It is lower at high altitude — which is why it is noticeably lower on the highlands around Addis Ababa than at sea level.

**Floating and sinking:** When an object is in a fluid, the fluid pushes up on it with a force called **upthrust** (or buoyant force). An object **floats** if it is less dense than the fluid and **sinks** if it is denser. A steel nail sinks, but a steel ship floats because its overall shape makes its *average* density less than water.

**Why pressure spreads in liquids:** Because liquid particles can move, a push is passed equally in all directions — this is the idea behind hydraulic machines.

sections.title: Worked example: pressure under a box and in water
sections.body:
**Question:** (a) A box weighs 200 N and rests on an area of 0.5 m². Find the pressure it exerts. (b) Find the water pressure at a depth of 4 m (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 10 m/s²).

**Step 1 — Pressure of the box using P = F / A.**
P = 200 N ÷ 0.5 m² = **400 Pa**

**Step 2 — Water pressure using P = ρgh.**
P = 1000 × 10 × 4
P = **40 000 Pa**

**Answer:** The box exerts 400 Pa, and the water pressure at 4 m depth is 40 000 Pa (= 40 kPa).

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body:
- **Confusing force and pressure.** The same force gives different pressures on different areas.
- **Thinking deeper water has more pressure because there is 'more water sideways'.** Pressure depends on depth (h), not the width of the container.
- **Forgetting liquid pressure acts in all directions**, not just downward.
- **Mixing up cm² and m²** in P = F/A — convert area to m² first.
- **Saying heavy objects always sink.** It is *density*, not weight, that decides floating.

sections.title: Memory tips
sections.body:
- **P = F/A:** "Pressure = Force per Area." Small area → big pressure (think sharp knife).
- **P = ρgh** for liquids: deeper = denser push. "Rho-g-h: Really Great Height."
- Pascal = newton per square metre (N/m²).
- **Floats if less dense, sinks if denser** than the fluid.
- A drawing pin: tiny tip area means huge pressure — that's how it pierces.

sections.title: Practice questions
sections.body:
Try these, then check the answers (use g = 10 m/s²).

**Q1.** A force of 60 N acts on an area of 0.2 m². Find the pressure.
**Q2.** Find the pressure at 5 m depth in water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³).
**Q3.** An object has a density of 1200 kg/m³. Will it float or sink in water (1000 kg/m³)?

**Answers:**
1. P = F/A = 60 ÷ 0.2 = **300 Pa**
2. P = ρgh = 1000 × 10 × 5 = **50 000 Pa**
3. It is denser than water, so it will **sink**.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
- **Pressure** P = F/A, measured in **pascals (Pa)**; small area gives big pressure.
- A **fluid** is anything that flows (liquids and gases).
- **Liquid pressure** P = ρgh increases with depth and density and acts in all directions.
- **Atmospheric pressure** is caused by the weight of air (~101 000 Pa at sea level), lower at altitude.
- **Upthrust** pushes objects up in a fluid.
- An object **floats** if less dense than the fluid and **sinks** if denser.

flashcards.back: P = ρgh (density × g × depth)

questions.explanation: Pressure is measured in pascals (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N/m².

questions.explanation: Liquid pressure P = ρgh depends only on depth and density (and g), not on the shape or width of the container.

questions.explanation: An object floats if it is less dense than the fluid. 800 kg/m³ is less than 1000 kg/m³, so it floats.

options: There is less air above pushing down
questions.explanation: Atmospheric pressure comes from the weight of air above. At higher altitude there is less air above, so the pressure is lower.

chapters.title: Temperature and Heat
chapters.description: The difference between temperature and heat, thermal expansion, and how heat is transferred.

lessons.title: Temperature, Heat and Heat Transfer
lessons.summary: Learn the difference between temperature and heat, how to convert temperature scales, thermal expansion, and the three ways heat moves.

sections.title: Hot and cold
sections.body:
On a warm afternoon in Dire Dawa you feel hot; in the cool highland nights you feel cold. But what is really happening? **Temperature** tells us how hot or cold something is, while **heat** is the energy that flows from a hotter object to a colder one.

Understanding heat explains everyday things: why a metal spoon in hot shiro gets hot at the handle, why we leave gaps in metal bridges, and why a pot of water boils. This lesson separates these two ideas and shows how heat moves.

sections.title: What you will learn
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- Explain the difference between **temperature** and **heat**.
- Convert between **Celsius** and **Kelvin** scales.
- Describe **thermal expansion** of solids, liquids and gases.
- Explain the three methods of heat transfer: **conduction**, **convection** and **radiation**.
- Give everyday examples of each.

sections.title: Temperature, heat and how heat moves
sections.body:
**Temperature** is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance — how fast they move. Its SI unit is the **kelvin (K)**, but we often use **degrees Celsius (°C)**.

To convert: **K = °C + 273**. So 0 °C = 273 K, and 100 °C = 373 K. The lowest possible temperature, **absolute zero**, is 0 K (−273 °C).

**Heat** is energy that flows from a hotter body to a colder body because of the temperature difference. Heat is measured in **joules (J)**. *Temperature is not the same as heat:* a cup of boiling water has a higher temperature than a warm lake, but the lake holds far more heat energy because it has so much more water.

**Thermal expansion:** Most substances **expand** when heated and **contract** when cooled, because the particles move more and take up more space. Gases expand most, then liquids, then solids. This is why engineers leave small gaps between sections of railway lines and bridges so they do not buckle in the heat.

**Three ways heat is transferred:**

1. **Conduction** — heat passes through a solid from particle to particle, without the material moving. Metals are good conductors; wood and air are poor conductors (insulators). A metal spoon handle gets hot by conduction.
2. **Convection** — heat moves through liquids and gases as the warmer, less dense fluid rises and cooler fluid sinks, forming a current. This is how a pot of water heats up and how breezes form.
3. **Radiation** — heat travels as invisible waves (infrared) and needs no material at all. This is how heat from the Sun reaches Earth across empty space.

**Why these differ:** Conduction needs touching particles, convection needs a flowing fluid, and radiation needs nothing at all — each suits different situations.

sections.title: Worked example: temperature conversion
sections.body:
**Question:** (a) Convert 37 °C (human body temperature) to kelvin. (b) Convert 300 K to degrees Celsius.

**Step 1 — Recall the rule.** K = °C + 273.

**Step 2 — Convert 37 °C to kelvin.**
K = 37 + 273 = **310 K**

**Step 3 — Convert 300 K to °C.** Rearrange: °C = K − 273.
°C = 300 − 273 = **27 °C**

**Answer:** 37 °C = 310 K, and 300 K = 27 °C.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body:
- **Thinking temperature and heat are the same.** Temperature measures hotness; heat is energy that flows.
- **Subtracting when converting °C to K.** Add 273 to go from °C to K.
- **Saying radiation needs air.** Radiation travels through a vacuum (that's how sunlight reaches us).
- **Confusing conduction and convection.** Conduction is in solids; convection needs a flowing fluid.
- **Forgetting gases expand more than solids** when heated.

sections.title: Memory tips
sections.body:
- **K = °C + 273:** "Kelvin is Celsius plus 273."
- **Three transfers:** **C-C-R** → **C**onduction (solids), **C**onvection (fluids), **R**adiation (no medium).
- **Convection = currents** (both start with C and involve flow).
- **Radiation reaches across space** — think of the Sun.
- Heat flows from **hot to cold**, never the other way on its own.

sections.title: Practice questions
sections.body:
Try these, then check the answers.

**Q1.** Convert 25 °C to kelvin.
**Q2.** Convert 350 K to degrees Celsius.
**Q3.** By which method does heat from the Sun reach the Earth?

**Answers:**
1. 25 + 273 = **298 K**
2. 350 − 273 = **77 °C**
3. **Radiation** (it travels through empty space).

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
- **Temperature** measures the average kinetic energy of particles (kelvin or °C).
- **Heat** is energy that flows from hot to cold (joules); it is not the same as temperature.
- Convert with **K = °C + 273**; absolute zero is 0 K (−273 °C).
- **Thermal expansion:** substances expand when heated; gases expand most.
- Heat moves by **conduction** (solids), **convection** (fluids) and **radiation** (no medium needed).

questions.explanation: The kelvin (K) is the SI base unit of temperature. Degrees Celsius are commonly used but are not the SI base unit.

questions.explanation: Heat is energy that flows from a hotter body to a colder one. Temperature measures how hot something is.

questions.explanation: In a solid, heat passes from particle to particle by conduction. Metals are good conductors of heat.

questions.explanation: Steel expands when heated. The gaps allow the rails to expand in hot weather without buckling.

questions.explanation: Radiation travels as infrared waves and needs no material medium, so it can cross the vacuum of space from the Sun to Earth.

chapters.title: Wave Motion and Sound
chapters.description: What waves are, the properties of waves, and how sound travels and is heard.

lessons.title: Waves and Sound
lessons.summary: Learn the types and properties of waves, the wave equation, and how sound is produced, travels and is heard.

sections.title: Carrying energy without carrying matter
sections.body:
Drop a stone into a pool and ripples spread out, but a floating leaf only bobs up and down — it does not travel with the ripple. This is the key idea of a **wave**: a wave carries **energy** from one place to another *without* carrying the material itself.

Waves are everywhere — water waves, the sound of a *masinko*, light from a lamp, and radio signals. This lesson explains the kinds of waves, how we describe them, and how sound, a wave we hear every day, behaves.

sections.title: What you will learn
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- Define a **wave** and explain that it transfers energy.
- Distinguish **transverse** and **longitudinal** waves.
- Define **wavelength**, **frequency**, **period** and **amplitude**.
- Use the **wave equation** v = fλ.
- Explain how **sound** is produced and why it needs a medium.

sections.title: Wave types, properties and sound
sections.body:
A **wave** is a disturbance that carries energy from one place to another without transferring matter.

There are two main types:
- In a **transverse wave**, the particles vibrate *at right angles* to the direction the wave travels (e.g. water waves, light).
- In a **longitudinal wave**, the particles vibrate *along* the direction of travel, making compressions and rarefactions (e.g. sound).

Four properties describe any wave:
- **Wavelength (λ)** — the distance between two matching points (e.g. crest to crest), in metres.
- **Frequency (f)** — the number of waves passing a point each second, in **hertz (Hz)**.
- **Period (T)** — the time for one complete wave, in seconds. Frequency and period are linked by **T = 1/f**.
- **Amplitude** — the maximum distance a particle moves from its rest position; it shows the wave's energy.

These are connected by the **wave equation**:

**v = f λ**

where v = wave speed (m/s), f = frequency (Hz), λ = wavelength (m).

**Sound** is a longitudinal wave produced by a **vibrating** object, such as a drum skin or your vocal cords. Sound needs a **medium** (solid, liquid or gas) to travel — it cannot pass through a vacuum, which is why there is no sound in space. Sound travels faster in solids than in liquids, and faster in liquids than in gases, because the particles are closer together. In air it travels at about 340 m/s.

**Why amplitude and frequency matter for sound:** A bigger amplitude means a **louder** sound; a higher frequency means a **higher-pitched** sound.

sections.title: Worked example: using the wave equation
sections.body:
**Question:** A sound wave has a frequency of 170 Hz and travels at 340 m/s in air. (a) Find its wavelength. (b) Find its period.

**Step 1 — Write the wave equation.** v = fλ, so λ = v ÷ f.

**Step 2 — Find the wavelength.**
λ = 340 ÷ 170 = **2 m**

**Step 3 — Find the period using T = 1/f.**
T = 1 ÷ 170 ≈ **0.0059 s** (about 5.9 milliseconds)

**Answer:** The wavelength is 2 m and the period is about 0.0059 s.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body:
- **Thinking waves carry matter.** Waves carry energy; the medium only vibrates in place.
- **Mixing up frequency and wavelength.** Frequency is waves per second (Hz); wavelength is a distance (m).
- **Saying sound travels through a vacuum.** Sound needs a medium; only light and other electromagnetic waves cross a vacuum.
- **Confusing amplitude with wavelength.** Amplitude is the height (energy); wavelength is the length of one wave.
- **Forgetting to rearrange v = fλ** correctly when solving for λ or f.

sections.title: Memory tips
sections.body:
- **v = fλ:** "Velocity = frequency × wavelength."
- **Transverse = T for 'at a Turn'** (right angles); **Longitudinal = Lined up** (same direction).
- **Frequency in Hz = how Frequently** waves pass per second.
- **Amplitude = Aloudness:** bigger amplitude, louder sound.
- **Sound needs stuff** to travel — no air, no sound (space is silent).

sections.title: Practice questions
sections.body:
Try these, then check the answers.

**Q1.** A wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 4 m. Find its speed.
**Q2.** A wave travels at 300 m/s with a wavelength of 1.5 m. Find its frequency.
**Q3.** A wave has a frequency of 25 Hz. Find its period.

**Answers:**
1. v = fλ = 50 × 4 = **200 m/s**
2. f = v/λ = 300 ÷ 1.5 = **200 Hz**
3. T = 1/f = 1 ÷ 25 = **0.04 s**

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
- A **wave** transfers **energy** without transferring matter.
- **Transverse** waves vibrate at right angles to travel; **longitudinal** waves vibrate along it.
- Key properties: **wavelength** (m), **frequency** (Hz), **period** (s), **amplitude**.
- **Wave equation:** v = fλ; and T = 1/f.
- **Sound** is a longitudinal wave from a vibrating object and needs a medium; ~340 m/s in air.
- Bigger amplitude = louder; higher frequency = higher pitch.

The number of waves passing a point each second, measured in hertz (Hz).

The maximum distance a particle moves from its rest position; shows the wave's energy.

flashcards.back: Transverse: vibration at right angles to travel; longitudinal: vibration along the travel direction.

flashcards.back: Sound is a wave that needs a medium; space is a vacuum with no particles.

questions.explanation: A wave carries energy without carrying matter; the medium only vibrates in place.

questions.prompt: Sound is an example of which type of wave?
questions.explanation: Sound is a longitudinal wave: the particles vibrate back and forth along the direction the wave travels.

In which medium does sound travel fastest?
questions.explanation: Sound travels fastest in solids like steel because the particles are closest together and pass on the vibration quickly. It cannot travel in a vacuum at all.

questions.explanation: Amplitude is linked to energy, so a larger amplitude makes the sound louder. Pitch is controlled by frequency, not amplitude.

chapters.title: Light and Optics
chapters.description: How light behaves, reflection and refraction, and the formation of images by mirrors and lenses.

lessons.title: Light, Reflection and Refraction
lessons.summary: Learn the nature and properties of light, the laws of reflection, how refraction bends light, and how mirrors and lenses form images.

sections.title: Seeing the world
sections.body:
We see everything around us because of **light**. Light from the Sun or a lamp bounces off objects and enters our eyes. **Light** is a form of energy that travels in straight lines and can move through empty space.

Light explains why a mirror shows your face, why a stick looks bent when dipped in water, and how spectacles help people see clearly. This lesson covers how light travels, reflects and refracts, and how mirrors and lenses make images.

sections.title: What you will learn
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- Describe key properties of **light**.
- State the **laws of reflection**.
- Explain **refraction** and why light bends.
- Distinguish **real** and **virtual** images.
- Describe images formed by **plane mirrors** and **lenses**.

sections.title: Reflection, refraction and images
sections.body:
**Light** is a form of energy that travels in straight lines (called **rays**) at a very high speed — about 3 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum, the fastest speed in the universe. Light can travel through a vacuum, which is why sunlight reaches Earth.

**Reflection** is when light bounces off a surface. The **laws of reflection** are:
1. The **angle of incidence** equals the **angle of reflection** (both measured from the **normal**, an imaginary line at right angles to the surface).
2. The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal all lie in the same plane.

A smooth surface like a mirror gives a clear (**regular**) reflection; a rough surface scatters light (**diffuse** reflection).

**Refraction** is the bending of light when it passes from one transparent material into another (e.g. from air into water), because light changes speed. Light slows down and bends *towards* the normal when entering a denser medium (like glass), and speeds up and bends *away* when leaving it. This is why a straw in a glass of water looks bent.

**Images** can be of two kinds:
- A **real image** is formed where rays actually meet and can be caught on a screen (e.g. the image in a film projector).
- A **virtual image** only appears to be there and cannot be caught on a screen (e.g. your reflection in a flat mirror).

A **plane mirror** forms an image that is virtual, upright, the same size as the object, and as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. **Lenses** are shaped glass that refract light: a **convex (converging)** lens can form real or virtual images and is used in magnifying glasses and the eye; a **concave (diverging)** lens spreads light out.

**Why light bends:** A change in speed at the boundary changes the direction of the ray — the deeper reason behind lenses, prisms and rainbows.

sections.title: Reflection from a plane mirror
sections.body: When a ray of light hits a mirror, it reflects so that the **angle of incidence** (between the incoming ray and the normal) equals the **angle of reflection** (between the normal and the outgoing ray). The normal is the dashed line drawn at right angles to the mirror at the point where the ray strikes.

sections.title: Worked example: angle of reflection
sections.body:
**Question:** A ray of light strikes a plane mirror so that it makes an angle of 30° with the mirror surface. Find (a) the angle of incidence and (b) the angle of reflection.

**Step 1 — Remember angles are measured from the normal.** The normal is at 90° to the mirror. The ray makes 30° with the *surface*, so it makes 90° − 30° = 60° with the normal.

**Step 2 — State the angle of incidence.** The angle of incidence (from the normal) = **60°**.

**Step 3 — Apply the law of reflection.** Angle of reflection = angle of incidence = **60°**.

**Answer:** Both the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection are 60°.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body:
- **Measuring angles from the surface instead of the normal.** Always measure from the normal.
- **Thinking a plane mirror image is real.** It is virtual — it cannot be caught on a screen.
- **Confusing reflection and refraction.** Reflection = bouncing off; refraction = bending while passing through.
- **Saying light needs a medium like sound does.** Light travels through a vacuum.
- **Mixing up convex and concave lenses.** Convex converges (brings light together); concave diverges.

sections.title: Memory tips
sections.body:
- **Law of reflection:** angle **i**n = angle **out** (i = r), measured from the **normal**.
- **Refraction = Ray changes speed** at a boundary, so it bends.
- **Real image = caught on a screen; Virtual = only Visible, not catchable.**
- **Convex Converges** (both have a 'C-then-together' feel); **concave** spreads out.
- Light is the fastest thing there is: 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

sections.title: Practice questions
sections.body:
Try these, then check the answers.

**Q1.** A ray hits a mirror at an angle of incidence of 35°. What is the angle of reflection?
**Q2.** Why does a stick look bent when partly dipped in water?
**Q3.** Is the image in a flat bathroom mirror real or virtual?

**Answers:**
1. By the law of reflection, angle of reflection = **35°**.
2. Because of **refraction** — light bends as it leaves the water, so the stick appears bent.
3. **Virtual** — it cannot be projected onto a screen.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
- **Light** is energy that travels in straight rays at ~3 × 10⁸ m/s and can cross a vacuum.
- **Reflection:** angle of incidence = angle of reflection (measured from the normal).
- **Refraction:** light bends when it changes speed passing between media.
- A **real image** can be caught on a screen; a **virtual image** cannot.
- A **plane mirror** gives a virtual, upright, same-size image.
- **Convex lenses converge** light; **concave lenses diverge** it.

flashcards.back: A real image can be caught on a screen; a virtual image cannot.

lessons.title: Static Electricity and Charge
lessons.summary: Learn about electric charge, how objects gain charge by friction, conductors and insulators, and the forces between charges.

sections.title: The crackle of static
sections.body:
Have you ever rubbed a plastic pen on your hair and used it to pick up tiny pieces of paper? Or felt a small shock touching a metal door after walking on a carpet? This is **static electricity** — electric charge that builds up and stays in one place.

All of this comes from **electric charge**, one of the basic properties of matter. Understanding charge is the first step to understanding electric current, which powers our homes and phones. This lesson explains charge and the forces between charges.

sections.title: What you will learn
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- Describe the two types of **electric charge**.
- Explain how objects become charged by **friction**.
- State the **law of charges** (like and unlike).
- Distinguish **conductors** and **insulators**.
- Explain charging by **induction** in simple terms.

sections.title: Charge, charging and forces
sections.body:
Matter is made of atoms, which contain positive **protons** and negative **electrons**. **Electric charge** is a basic property of these particles. There are two kinds: **positive (+)** and **negative (−)**. The SI unit of charge is the **coulomb (C)**.

Normally an atom has equal protons and electrons, so it is **neutral**. An object becomes **charged** when it gains or loses **electrons** (protons stay fixed in the nucleus):
- Gaining electrons makes an object **negatively** charged.
- Losing electrons makes an object **positively** charged.

**Charging by friction:** When two different materials are rubbed together, electrons move from one to the other. For example, rubbing a plastic rod with a cloth can transfer electrons to the rod, leaving it negative and the cloth positive. Charge is never created or destroyed, only transferred — this is **conservation of charge**.

**The law of charges:** **Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.** Two negative objects push apart, while a positive and a negative object pull together. This force between charges is called the **electrostatic force**.

**Conductors and insulators:**
- A **conductor** lets charge (electrons) move through it easily — e.g. metals like copper, and the human body.
- An **insulator** does not let charge move easily — e.g. plastic, rubber, dry wood, glass.

**Charging by induction:** A charged object brought *near* a neutral conductor can rearrange its charges (pulling opposite charges to the near side) without touching it, producing attraction. This is how a charged pen attracts neutral pieces of paper.

**Why opposite charges attract:** Positive and negative are opposites that pull together, just as two norths of a magnet push apart — a basic rule of electricity.

sections.title: Worked example: predicting the force
sections.body:
**Question:** A plastic rod is rubbed with a cloth and becomes negatively charged. (a) What charge does the cloth have? (b) If this rod is brought near another negatively charged rod, will they attract or repel? (c) What about near a positively charged rod?

**Step 1 — Use conservation of charge for the cloth.** The rod gained electrons (negative), so the cloth must have lost the same electrons. The cloth is therefore **positively** charged.

**Step 2 — Apply the law of charges for two negative rods.** Like charges repel, so the two negative rods **repel**.

**Step 3 — Apply the law for negative and positive.** Unlike charges attract, so the negative rod and the positive rod **attract**.

**Answer:** (a) The cloth is positive. (b) They repel. (c) They attract.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body:
- **Thinking protons move during charging.** Only electrons move; protons stay in the nucleus.
- **Saying gaining charge means gaining protons.** Gaining electrons makes an object negative.
- **Mixing up the law of charges.** Like repel, unlike attract — not the other way round.
- **Believing charge is created by rubbing.** It is only *transferred*; total charge is conserved.
- **Confusing conductors and insulators.** Metals conduct; plastic and rubber insulate.

sections.title: Memory tips
sections.body:
- **Like charges Leave (repel); unlike charges Unite (attract).**
- **Only electrons move** — "electrons are the runners, protons stay home."
- **Gain electrons → go negative; lose electrons → go positive.**
- **Conductors carry charge** (metals); **insulators isolate** it (plastic, rubber).
- Unit of charge = **coulomb (C)**.

sections.title: Practice questions
sections.body:
Try these, then check the answers.

**Q1.** An object loses electrons. What charge does it now have?
**Q2.** Two positively charged balloons are brought close. Do they attract or repel?
**Q3.** Name one good conductor and one good insulator.

**Answers:**
1. **Positive** (losing electrons leaves more protons than electrons).
2. They **repel** (like charges repel).
3. Conductor: **copper (a metal)**; insulator: **plastic (or rubber)**.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
- **Electric charge** is positive or negative; its unit is the **coulomb (C)**.
- Objects charge by **gaining or losing electrons**; protons do not move.
- **Conservation of charge:** charge is transferred, not created or destroyed.
- **Law of charges:** like charges repel, unlike charges attract.
- **Conductors** (metals) let charge flow; **insulators** (plastic, rubber) do not.
- A charged object can attract a neutral one by **induction**.

lessons.title: Current, Voltage and Ohm's Law
lessons.summary: Learn what electric current, voltage and resistance are, how to use Ohm's law, and the difference between series and parallel circuits.

sections.title: Electricity that flows
sections.body:
When you switch on a lamp or charge a phone, **electric current** flows through wires. Unlike static electricity that stays still, current is charge that **moves**. Current electricity powers homes, schools and the lights of Addis Ababa.

To control electricity safely, we need three key ideas: **current** (how much charge flows), **voltage** (what pushes it) and **resistance** (what slows it down). They are linked by a simple and powerful rule called **Ohm's law**. This lesson puts them together and builds simple circuits.

sections.title: What you will learn
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- Define **electric current**, **voltage** and **resistance** with their units.
- State and use **Ohm's law**, V = IR.
- Identify the main **circuit components** and their symbols.
- Compare **series** and **parallel** circuits.
- Solve simple circuit problems.

sections.title: Current, voltage, resistance and Ohm's law
sections.body:
**Electric current (I)** is the rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor. Its SI unit is the **ampere (A)**. A current flows only in a complete (closed) circuit.

**Voltage (V)**, also called potential difference, is the 'push' that drives the current around the circuit. It is provided by a cell or battery and measured in **volts (V)**.

**Resistance (R)** is how much a component opposes the flow of current. It is measured in **ohms (Ω)**. A thin or long wire has more resistance than a thick or short one.

These three are connected by **Ohm's law**:

**V = I R**

where V = voltage (V), I = current (A), R = resistance (Ω). From this we can also write I = V/R and R = V/I. Ohm's law lets us calculate any one of the three if we know the other two.

**Common circuit components and symbols:**
- **Cell/battery** — provides voltage.
- **Bulb/lamp** — gives light when current flows.
- **Switch** — opens or closes the circuit.
- **Resistor** — controls the current.
- **Wire** — carries the current.

**Series and parallel circuits:**
- In a **series** circuit, components are joined end-to-end in a single loop. The same current flows through each component, but the voltage is shared. If one bulb fails, the whole circuit breaks.
- In a **parallel** circuit, components are on separate branches. Each branch gets the full voltage, and if one bulb fails the others keep working. Home wiring uses parallel connections.

**Why Ohm's law matters:** It is the single most useful rule in electricity, letting us design circuits that deliver the right current safely.

sections.title: A simple series circuit
sections.body: This simple circuit has a 1.5 V cell connected to a lamp by wires. When the circuit is complete, the cell pushes a current around the loop and the lamp lights. Adding a switch would let us open the loop to turn the lamp off.

sections.title: Worked example: using Ohm's law
sections.body:
**Question:** A lamp of resistance 6 Ω is connected to a 12 V battery. (a) Find the current through the lamp. (b) If the resistance were doubled to 12 Ω with the same battery, what current flows?

**Step 1 — Write Ohm's law and rearrange for current.** V = IR, so I = V ÷ R.

**Step 2 — Find the current for 6 Ω.**
I = 12 V ÷ 6 Ω = **2 A**

**Step 3 — Find the current for 12 Ω.**
I = 12 V ÷ 12 Ω = **1 A**

**Answer:** The current is 2 A at 6 Ω and 1 A at 12 Ω. Doubling the resistance halves the current (for the same voltage).

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body:
- **Mixing up the units.** Current = amperes (A), voltage = volts (V), resistance = ohms (Ω).
- **Rearranging Ohm's law wrongly.** From V = IR: I = V/R and R = V/I.
- **Thinking current is 'used up' in a circuit.** The same current flows all around a simple series loop.
- **Confusing series and parallel.** Series = one loop; parallel = separate branches.
- **Forgetting a circuit must be complete (closed)** for current to flow.

sections.title: Memory tips
sections.body:
- **Ohm's law triangle:** put V on top, I and R below. Cover the one you want: V = I × R, I = V/R, R = V/I.
- **Units: A-V-O** → **A**mpere (current), **V**olt (voltage), **O**hm (resistance).
- **Series = Single path** (one loop); **Parallel = several branches**.
- In **parallel**, one bulb out, the rest stay on — like home lighting.
- No closed loop, no current.

sections.title: Practice questions
sections.body:
Try these, then check the answers.

**Q1.** A 4 Ω resistor carries a current of 3 A. What is the voltage across it?
**Q2.** A 9 V battery drives current through a 3 Ω resistor. Find the current.
**Q3.** In a series circuit, if one bulb burns out, what happens to the others?

**Answers:**
1. V = IR = 3 × 4 = **12 V**
2. I = V/R = 9 ÷ 3 = **3 A**
3. They all **go out**, because the single loop is broken.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
- **Current (I)** is the flow of charge, in **amperes (A)**; it needs a closed circuit.
- **Voltage (V)** is the push from a cell, in **volts (V)**.
- **Resistance (R)** opposes current, in **ohms (Ω)**.
- **Ohm's law:** V = IR (also I = V/R, R = V/I).
- **Series** circuits share one loop (same current); **parallel** circuits have separate branches (same voltage).
- In parallel, one component failing does not stop the others.
